title: Do Not Drag Me, Time. Leave Me...
text:
Do not drag me, time. Leave me

forgotten in a corner.

Do not wound me like this, piercing through me;

let me sleep peacefully

one night, even once,

knowing that you are not stealing

my dreams from me piece by piece.

Do not deprive the perfume

of the flower that sustains it.

If you wear out the violin's strings, time,

they will break when music

wants to vibrate in them.

Late I learned that I could,

like a flower,

open myself toward life,

and I have not yet blossomed.

Time—please—wait.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the plea to time and the flower/violin images of delayed blossoming.

title: The Appearance
text:
Things, for being known,

do not stop astonishing us.

The sun is shining,

people in the streets

stroll, eat ice cream;

children run, play,

and there are roses in the courtyards.

As if death were not passing by,

swallowing the streets,

and the Mapocho River were not running

with such strange fish.

Nothing. The sun shines and, as always,

people in the streets.

But a little before curfew

a general stampede breaks

this appearance.

And it is like a cruel relief

to know that they know.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the everyday surface of Chile under curfew and the cruel relief when fear reveals shared knowledge.

title: Stacked Sorrows
text:
I will say it at the start

for whoever wants to understand:

they are sorrows piled high,

to be poor and be a woman.


She works her whole life

barely enough to eat.

She has the sorrows of the poor

and, on top of that, those of being a woman.


The rich woman has rights,

the poor woman has duties.

It is already much to suffer for being poor

and on top of that for being a woman.


She is so helpless

and is mother and father at once.

Rights, not even the right to complain,

for being poor and being a woman.


Many speeches are made

about her heroism of yesterday.

On paper they respect her.

But only on paper.


And I repeat it again

for whoever wants to understand:

they are sorrows piled high,

to be poor and be a woman.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated, songlike indictment of class and gender oppression.

title: Wings and Chains
text:
Hear me. I have seen.

There is blood in the ears of grain

and blood in the clods,

and the wounds

are full of earth and full

of seeds that germinate.


I have seen

boot prints that have passed through,

breaking the cornfields,

and forbidden voices haranguing

rebellious manioc fields.


I have seen

the little sword of the palm rise angrily,

seeking someone to wield it,

and hands stretched out in search of it,

bleeding on the thorns.


I have seen

the swollen furrow break open,

full of potential forces,

with tremors arriving unbridled

from the quebracho groves.


I have seen

the fury of the wind redoubling

its rages with its sorrows.

And hear me.

The earth is forging

its wings, without chains.
editorial_note: The translation keeps Soler's agricultural uprising imagery, with earth, crops, and quebracho groves becoming insurgent.

title: Antonio Maidana
text:
His name is Antonio,

as he might be named

Agüero,

Mariano Roque Alonso,

Alberto Candia,

Alonso Ramírez,

Juan Carlos Rivas,

Juan Mora,

Mariano Jara,

Miguel Ángel Soler,

Derlis Villagra,

Rubén González Acosta,

Emio Roa and so many,

so many! others.

But his name is Antonio,

unique Antonio

of the thick wall

of the dark cell

that could not defeat him

in 20 years

of "pantheons for the living"

in the 3rd Police Station,

in the camp of "Emboscada."

His name is

and will forever be called

Antonio Maidana,

Antonio whole,

Antonio Quebracho,

as the people call him,

who receive his example

in the night

of struggle

and waiting.

The only Antonio named

when one says light, quebracho, strength.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the roll call of political prisoners and Antonio Maidana's symbolic name as light, quebracho, and strength.
